'''''Gracilaria''''', also known as '''Irish moss''' or '''ogonori''',<ref name="seaweedinsights1">{{cite web |title=Gracilaria spp. |url=https://seaweedinsights.com/global-production-gracilaria/ |website=Seaweed Insights |publisher=Hatch Innovation Services |access-date=24 April 2024 |ref=seaweedinsights1 |archive-date=1 March 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250301103502/https://seaweedinsights.com/global-production-gracilaria/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> is a genus of [[red algae]] in the family [[Gracilariaceae]]. It is notable for its economic importance as an [[agarophyte]] meaning that it is used to make [[agar]], as well as its use as a food for humans and various species of shellfish. Various species in the genus are cultivated among [[Asia]], [[South America]], [[Africa]] and [[Oceania]]. They produce over 90% of the world's agar.<ref name="seaweedinsights1"/>

==Distribution==
''Gracilaria'' are found in warm waters throughout the world, though they also occur seasonally in temperate waters. It can not tolerate temperatures below {{convert|10|°C|°F|abbr=on}}.{{clarification needed|reason=which species does this refer to?|date=April 2023}} ''Gracilaria'' are found in all oceans except the [[Arctic Ocean|Arctic]]. Their center of diversity is the [[Western Pacific Ocean|Western Pacific]], where they have been traditionally cultivated as a source of [[agar]].<ref name="McLachlan">{{cite journal |last1=McLachlan |first1=J. |last2=Bird |first2=C.J. |title=Geographical and experimental assessment of the distribution of Gracilaria species (Rhodophyta: Gigartinales) in relation to temperature |journal=Helgoländer Meeresuntersuchungen  |date=1984 |volume=38 |issue=3–4 |pages=319–334 |doi=10.1007/BF02027684 |bibcode=1984HM.....38..319M |s2cid=20852797 |url=https://hmr.biomedcentral.com/track/pdf/10.1007/BF02027684.pdf}}</ref><ref name="Oliveira">{{cite book |last1=de Oliveira |first1=E.C. |last2=Plastino |first2=E.M. |editor-last=Akatsuka |editor-first=Isamu |title=Biology of Economic Algae |date=1994 |publisher=SPB Academic Publishing |chapter=Gracilariaceae |isbn=9789051030938}}</ref>

==Use==
[[Image:Ogo.jpg|thumb|Ogonori]]
[[File:Kkosiraegi-muchim.jpg|thumb|''Kkosiraegi-[[muchim]]'' (seasoned gracilaria)]]
''Gracilaria'' is used as a food in [[Filipino cuisine|Filipino]], [[Cuisine of Hawaii|Hawaiian]], [[Japanese cuisine|Japanese]], [[Korean cuisine|Korean]] and [[Sri Lankan cuisine]]s.<ref>Kyaw, Aye, [http://www.fao.org/docrep/field/009/ag155e/AG155E05.htm The Production of ''Gracilaria eduli'' in Burma],  Report of the Training Course on Gracilaria Algae, Manila, Philippines, 1–30 April 1981, accessed 27 April 2013</ref><ref name="GracilariaSriLanka">{{Cite book | last1=Subasinghe | first1=S | last2=Jayasuriya | first2=A | title=Gracilaria Production and Utilization in the Bay of Bengal: Report of a Seminar Held in Songkhla, Thailand, 23-27 October 1989 | year= 1990| publisher= Bay of Bengal Programme for Fisheries Development, 1990 | pages=72}}</ref> In Japanese cuisine, it is called ''ogonori'' or ''ogo'', and used to make ''[[tokoroten]]''. In the [[Philippines]], it is called ''[[gulaman]]'' and used to make a [[Gelatin dessert|gelatin]] substitute.<ref>{{Cite book | last=Davidson | first=Alan | author-link=Alan Davidson (food writer) | title=Seafood of South-East Asia: A Comprehensive Guide with Recipes | year= 2004| publisher=[[Ten Speed Press]] | isbn=978-1-58008-452-9 | pages=197}}</ref> In [[Jamaica]], it is known as ''Irish moss''.<ref name="GoreauTrench2013">{{cite book|author1=Thomas J. Goreau|author2=Robert Kent Trench|title=Innovative Methods of Marine Ecosystem Restoration|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n8PoPCUZTTAC&pg=PA193|access-date=30 June 2013|year=2013|publisher=CRC Press|isbn=978-1-4665-5773-4|pages=193–}}</ref> In Korea, it is known as ''kkosiraegi''.

''Gracilaria'' [[oligosaccharide]]s with [[degree of polymerization]] 6 prepared by [[agarase]] digestion from agar-bearing ''Gracilaria'' sp. [[polysaccharide]]s have been shown to be an effective prophylactic agent during ''[[in vitro]]'' and ''[[in vivo]]'' experiments against [[Japanese encephalitis]] viral infection. The sulfated oligosaccharides from ''Gracilaria'' sp. seem to be promising candidates for further development as antiviral agents.<ref>{{cite journal |vauthors=Kazłowski B, Chiu YH, Kazłowska K, Pan CL, Wu CJ |title=Prevention of Japanese encephalitis virus infections by low-degree-polymerisation sulfated saccharides from ''Gracilaria'' sp. and ''Monostroma nitidum'' |journal=Food Chem |volume=133 |issue=3 |pages=866–74 |date=August 2012 |doi=10.1016/j.foodchem.2012.01.106 }}</ref>

In the [[Philippines]], ''Gracilaria'' have been harvested and used as food for centuries, eaten both fresh or sun-dried and turned into jellies. The earliest historical attestation is from the ''[[Vocabulario de la lengua tagala]]'' (1754) by the [[Jesuit]] priests Juan de Noceda and Pedro de Sanlucar, where ''golaman'' or ''gulaman'' was defined as ''"una yerva, de que se haze conserva a modo de Halea, naze en la mar"'' ("an herb, from which a jam-like preserve is made, grows in the sea"), with an additional entry for ''guinolaman'' to refer to food made with the jelly.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Albert H. Wells |title=Possibilities of Gulaman Dagat as a Substitute for Gelatin in Food |journal=The Philippine Journal of Science |date=1916 |volume=11 |pages=267–271}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=de Noceda |first1=Juan |last2=de Sanlucar |first2=Pedro |title=Vocabulario de la lengua Tagala |date=1754 |publisher=Imprenta de la compañia de Jesus |pages=101, 215}}</ref>

In Japan, ''Gracilaria'' has been used to produce ''funori'' ({{lang|ja|府海苔}}), an agar-based glue, since the 17th century.<ref name="aic">{{cite journal |last1=Swider |first1=Joseph R. |last2=Smith |first2=Martha |title=Funori: Overview of a 300-Year-Old Consolidant |journal=Journal of the American Institute for Conservation |date=2005 |volume=44 |issue=2 |pages=117–126 |doi=10.1179/019713605806082329 |s2cid=191358224 |url=https://cool.culturalheritage.org/jaic/articles/jaic44-02-005.html |access-date=9 April 2022|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In Sri Lanka, ''Gracilaria'' has been used to make a seaweed soup that also incorporates coconut cream and lime.<ref name="GracilariaSriLanka"/> It is also used to create seaweed jelly, a local sweetmeat in the [[Puttalam District]] of northwestern Sri Lanka.<ref name="GracilariaSriLanka"/>

Irish moss has long been used as a clarifying agent during the brewing of beer, especially among home brewers, as an alternative to mechanical filtering.<ref>{{cite web |title=Take the Luck out of Clear Beer with Irish Moss| url=https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gracilaria&action=edit&section=3https://www.homebrewersassociation.org/how-to-brew/take-the-luck-out-of-clear-beer-with-irish-moss/ |access-date=28 Nov 2024}}</ref>

''[[Gracilaria tikvahiae]]'' has been used as a model species to determine how well seaweed could be used as a [[resilient food]] in sun-blocking scenarios like [[nuclear winter]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Jehn |first1=Florian Ulrich |last2=Dingal |first2=Farrah Jasmine |last3=Mill |first3=Aron |last4=Harrison |first4=Cheryl |last5=Ilin |first5=Ekaterina |last6=Roleda |first6=Michael Y. |last7=James |first7=Scott C. |last8=Denkenberger |first8=David |title=Seaweed as a Resilient Food Solution After a Nuclear War |journal=Earth's Future |date=January 2024 |volume=12 |issue=1 |doi=10.1029/2023EF003710|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Aquarium trade==
''Gracilaria'' commonly appears as a macroalgae for sale in the aquarium trade. It is highly palatable to [[Acanthuridae|tangs]]<ref>{{cite web |quote = This brings me back to Achilles’s diet. The guy apparently really likes Gracilaria macro algae. No wonder, especially considering that the grass is indigenous to Hawaii as well, and is considered the favorite food for tangs. |url = https://saltwaterreefing.wordpress.com/2013/09/27/growing-gracilaria-parvispora/ |title = Growing Gracilaria Parvispora |publisher = Salt Water Reefing |first = Alex |last = Volynkin |access-date = 2016-12-18|date = 2013-09-28 }}</ref> and many other herbivorous fish, and its nutrient uptake ability makes it a suitable choice for a [[Refugium (fishkeeping)|refugium]].{{Cn|date=October 2024}}

==Ecology==
''Gracilaria'' are susceptible to infection by the [[Parasitism|parasitic]] oomycete ''[[Pythium porphyrae]]''.<ref name="Spencer">{{cite journal|last1=Spencer|first1=M. A.|title=Pythium porphyrae. (Descriptions of Fungi and Bacteria)|journal=IMI Descriptions of Fungi and Bacteria|date=2004|volume=162|issue=Sheet 1617|url=http://www.cabi.org/dfb/abstract/20056401617|access-date=10 October 2017|language=en|quote=A description is provided for Pythium porphyrae. Information is included on the disease caused by the organism, its transmission, geographical distribution, and hosts. DISEASES: Red-rot disease, red-wasting disease. HOSTS: Bangia atropurpurea, Callophyllis adhaerens, Polyopes affinis (syn}}</ref> Reproduction by ''Gracilaria gracilis'' is supported by ''[[Idotea balthica]]'' – the first known case of an animal helping algae reproduce.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Roth |first1=Annie |title=Like Bees of the Seas, These Crustaceans Pollinate Seaweed |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2022/07/28/science/pollination-algae-crustacean.html |access-date=21 August 2022 |work=The New York Times |date=28 July 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lavaut |first1=E. |last2=Guillemin |first2=M.-L. |last3=Colin |first3=S. |last4=Faure |first4=A. |last5=Coudret |first5=J. |last6=Destombe |first6=C. |last7=Valero |first7=M. |title=Pollinators of the sea: A discovery of animal-mediated fertilization in seaweed |journal=Science |date=29 July 2022 |volume=377 |issue=6605 |pages=528–530 |doi=10.1126/science.abo6661 |pmid=35901149 |bibcode=2022Sci...377..528L |s2cid=251159505 |language=en |issn=0036-8075|url=https://hal.science/hal-03740649/file/Lavaut_Science_2022_version%20Hal.pdf }}</ref><!--according to a 2022 study after [[pollination]] in the sea was first reported in 2016.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=van Tussenbroek |first1=Brigitta I. |last2=Villamil |first2=Nora |last3=Márquez-Guzmán |first3=Judith |last4=Wong |first4=Ricardo |last5=Monroy-Velázquez |first5=L. Verónica |last6=Solis-Weiss |first6=Vivianne |title=Experimental evidence of pollination in marine flowers by invertebrate fauna |journal=Nature Communications |date=29 September 2016 |volume=7 |issue=1 |pages=12980 |doi=10.1038/ncomms12980 |language=en |issn=2041-1723|doi-access=free}}</ref>-->
